item.title: Como, traffic disaster: open lanes and ZTL
item.description: The Municipality of Como has opened preferential lanes and ZTL zones for vehicles to Switzerland. Here are the authorized routes and how to move around the construction site.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - Construction site on Como Lakefront: underground services being redone; priority lanes and ZTL open - Vehicles heading to Switzerland can use via Rodari–piazza Roma–piazza Cavour–via Cairoli - Disruptions on the Lariana (Como-Bellagio); nine mayors have protested
## Key facts - **What**: Opening of priority lanes (via Sauro, Battisti, Milano) + ZTL passable for vehicles heading to Switzerland - When: For two days; end not yet specified - Where: Como, Lakefront; Lariana road Como-Bellagio - Who: Municipality of Como, mayors of the East shore of the lake, Acus - ZTL route: via Rodari–piazza Roma–via Bianchi Giovini–piazza Cavour–via Fontana–via Cairoli
### The construction site that paralyzes the passage to Switzerland The construction site started two days ago on the Como Lakefront for the renovation of underground services is causing devastating disruptions to normal traffic. The hole that opened months earlier made a deep structural intervention necessary, but the impact on traffic has been more severe than expected. The Lariana, the road connecting Como to Bellagio and one of the main traffic corridors to Ticino and the Chiasso border, is practically blocked. Italian cross-border workers who normally work in the Canton of Ticino usually travel this road to reach the border crossings. With the ongoing construction, the flow has completely jammed. The situation was so serious that nine mayors of the East shore of the lake sent a furious protest to the Municipality of Como and had even contacted the prefect to request intervention. Acus also reported the problem.
### The three priority lanes opened by the Municipality Faced with growing pressure, the Municipality of Como announced a series of temporary derogations from the normal traffic discipline, starting with the priority lanes. Until the completion of the lakefront works, the following priority lanes have been opened and made passable: - Via Sauro - Via Battisti - Via Milano, towards Milan Normally, priority lanes are reserved for buses, taxis, and vehicles with special permits. Opening them to ordinary vehicles represents a structured derogation, not an informal exception. This measure aims to increase the capacity of the road network in critical directions and to channel the flow through routes parallel to the blocked Lariana.
### Opening of the ZTL for traffic heading to Switzerland The most relevant measure for cross-border workers is the opening of a corridor through the Limited Traffic Zone (ZTL) of Como. Normally, the ZTL is closed to unauthorized vehicles, but during the construction phase, the Municipality has authorized passage for those heading to Switzerland, provided they follow a specific route: Via Rodari → Piazza Roma → Via Bianchi Giovini → Piazza Cavour → Via Fontana → Via Cairoli This route allows vehicles heading to the Swiss border crossings to cross Como without incurring penalties for violating the ZTL. The stated goal is to "ensure, compatibly with the necessary and unavoidable construction site, the greatest possible fluidity of traffic and contain the disruptions." The measures remain in effect until the completion of the works, the end of which has not yet been officially specified. ## Real impact on the cross-border commuter: times and routes
For the cross-border commuter who lives in Como or in the surrounding municipalities and works in Ticino, the construction site is not just local news. It is a concrete loss of time and potentially measurable in terms of hourly earnings. Those who normally take 15-20 minutes to travel the Lariana towards Chiasso now find themselves having to follow alternative routes that require precise navigation and add distance.
The choice between the priority lanes and the ZTL route is not intuitive. The priority lanes on via Sauro, Battisti, and Milano towards Milano can be useful for those coming from the north of the city, but for those living in central Como or in the lakeside municipalities and wanting to reach Chiasso, the added value is uncertain. The Lariana was the direct route; the alternatives revolve around the urban center, adding at least 5-10 minutes.
### How to navigate the ZTL route: dangers and procedures
The route via Rodari–piazza Roma–via Bianchi Giovini–piazza Cavour–via Fontana–via Cairoli is not the natural path. It requires knowing Como, following specific turns, and being careful not to exit the authorized route, risking a fine for violating the ZTL.
Many cross-border commuters do not know Como in detail and, relying on the navigator, might receive alternative suggestions that exit the authorized zone. In this case, a fine of several hundred euros could result from not respecting the ZTL exemption.
**Concrete actions**: Save the route on the navigator BEFORE having to travel it. Test the route during low traffic times (e.g., on the weekend) to familiarize yourself with the turns. Check on Google Maps or Apple Maps the real-time duration during peak hours compared to the departure with the Lariana free.
### Public transport as a structural alternative
If the construction site lasts more than two weeks, many cross-border commuters choose to abandon the car for the train. Como is served by two main stations (Como Lago and Como San Giovanni) with direct connections to Ticino via the regional Tilo trains. The journey Como–Chiasso–Lugano is covered by regular and reliable schedules, without traffic stress.
The cost of a weekly or monthly train subscription might be higher than fuel, but during the construction site, it represents an investment in punctuality. A cross-border commuter who takes 45 minutes instead of 20 is losing 25 minutes a day = 2 hours a week = 8 hours a month. If the gross hourly wage is higher than CHF 25, the cost of the delay exceeds CHF 200 monthly, making the train subscription economically convenient.
### When does the construction site end? A missing detail
The source does not specify when the Municipality of Como plans to complete the work. This is a critical element for the cross-border commuter: if the construction site lasts a week, it is worth adapting temporarily; if it lasts months, it is necessary to consider structural solutions (partial teleworking, flexible hours, permanent public transport). The Municipality should clearly communicate this date, but for the moment, it remains uncertain.
## Useful tools to protect your net income To reduce FX leakage, compare [CHF-EUR exchange options](nav:exchange) and [banks for cross-border workers](nav:banks). ## Practical procedure: what to do immediately
If you are a commuter leaving Como for Ticino during the construction period, follow this checklist:
1. Check the status of the construction site Contact the Municipality of Como or its official website to confirm if the construction site is still active and when it is expected to be completed. Do not rely solely on general news; call the Municipality's single number for up-to-date information.
2. Save the ZTL route on your navigator If you decide to use the route through the ZTL (via Rodari–piazza Roma–via Bianchi Giovini–piazza Cavour–via Fontana–via Cairoli), load it as a "saved route" on Google Maps or Apple Maps before you leave. This way, you will have step-by-step text and voice guidance.
3. Make a trial run during low traffic hours Drive the route once on the weekend or during peak hours to understand where the critical turns are, where the reference parking lots are, and what the actual travel time is.
**4. Compare total times** Calculate the total time from your home to the entrance of your employer in Ticino (or the Chiasso border crossing). Add: departure time + alternative route (e.g., ZTL with detours) + wait time at the border + arrival. If the delay is more than 30 minutes compared to the pre-construction situation, consider alternatives.
5. Consider telecommuting or flexible hours Contact your Swiss employer and explain the situation. Many cross-border contracts allow 1-2 days of telecommuting per week. Negotiating a partial week from home during the construction period may be more convenient than losing hours in traffic.
## Public transport: the savings calculator Trains Como–Chiasso–Lugano (operated by Tilo) guarantee fixed schedules and zero stress. The cost of a weekly pass is typically around CHF 60–80 for the Como–Chiasso zone. If your gross hourly wage is CHF 30 and you are losing 2 hours per week in traffic, the value of the lost time is CHF 60 per week, so the pass pays for itself.
[Consult the available public transport solutions to understand the schedules and costs of your route](nav:transport).
## The cost of delay in terms of salary A 30-minute daily delay corresponds to 2.5 hours lost per week. If your cross-border contract does not provide for weekly overtime recovery, you are effectively giving away time (and earnings). A useful tool is the [cross-border net salary calculator](nav:calculator): by entering your gross monthly salary and the number of hours lost per week in traffic, you can see how much the lost time is really worth in CHF and EUR.
If you find that the cost of the delay is higher than the alternative cost (e.g., rail pass, negotiated telecommuting), the economic choice is clear.
## Continuous monitoring of traffic at border crossings During the construction period, wait times at the Chiasso border crossing and other access points to Ticino may increase. [Regularly check the traffic history at the Ticino-Italy border crossings](nav:traffic-history) to understand if the bottleneck is shifting (e.g., from Como to the border) or if the Municipality's measures are actually working.
If the traffic at the border remains constant, it means that the alternative route in Como is working; if it increases, the problem has become systemic and it may be worth negotiating even more flexible hours with the employer or switching to a more permanent telecommuting solution for the construction period.

item.description: The Centre supports the financing of the 13th AVS annuity through a 0.4% VAT increase. Vote on 29 November. What changes for border workers?
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Centro Assembly approves AVS funding with 0.4% VAT increase - Swiss popular vote on 29 November - 164 votes in favor out of 183 delegates present
## Key facts - **What**: Centro Assembly supports funding of 13th AVS pension through VAT increase - When: 29 November (date of popular vote) - Where: Granges-Paccot, Canton of Fribourg - Who: 183 delegates of the Centro - Amount: VAT increase of 0.4 percentage points - Outcome: 164 votes in favor, 9 against, 10 abstentions
The Centro Assembly, meeting in Granges-Paccot in the Canton of Fribourg, expressed support for the additional funding of the AVS through an increase in the value-added tax (VAT). The vote recorded 164 votes in favor, 9 against, and 10 abstentions out of a total of 183 delegates. The proposed increase is 0.4 percentage points.
The decision concerns the funding of the 13th AVS pension, a measure that generates debates even within the party. Marie-France Roth Pasquier, a Fribourg national councillor, emphasized: "The 13th pension has been approved and must be funded." According to the politician, a rejection would not solve the structural problem of the pension system.
However, some delegates expressed significant concerns. They believe that the VAT-based model excessively penalizes the middle class. Furthermore, they argue that a different and more structural solution to the problem of Swiss pension funding is needed in the long term.
### The second item put to the vote
In addition to the AVS issue, the assembly unanimously approved the relaxation of restrictions on the export and re-export of military material. This revision has already been approved by the Federal Chambers. According to the Centro, a Switzerland capable of defending itself needs a solid industrial base and reliable international partnerships.
Both items will be put to the Swiss popular vote on 29 November. The 183 delegates present followed the party presidency's recommendations on both issues.
[Check your AVS situation](nav:pension) using the tools dedicated to cross-border commuters. ## What does this mean for cross-border commuters? For those who work in Switzerland and live in Italy, this decision has direct implications. The 0.4% increase in VAT affects the cost of living in Swiss territory, a relevant factor for cross-border commuters who travel daily across the border. However, the most significant aspect concerns the pension system itself.
### The AHV and mandatory contributions Cross-border commuters regularly pay AHV contributions on their Swiss paycheck. These contributions are mandatory and are withheld directly by the employer. Unlike some individual pension systems, the AHV operates on a solidarity basis: current workers finance today's retirees, with the expectation that tomorrow's workers will finance them.
The 13th AHV pension is an additional allowance paid once a year. For those with a limited pension income, this additional allowance can represent a significant contribution to the annual budget. Many cross-border retirees consider this amount part of their long-term financial planning.
### The impact of the VAT increase on daily expenses If the measure is approved in the vote on November 29, the 0.4% increase in VAT will be reflected in many goods and services purchased in Switzerland. For cross-border commuters, this is a matter of concrete budgeting: purchases of groceries in Ticino supermarkets, payment for services, medical services not covered by the LAMal, fuel — all will experience a slight increase.
Some representatives of the Center have suggested that other funding options could distribute the burden more fairly. Increases in mandatory contributions or revisions of federal tax rates could alternatively finance the system. However, the VAT method was preferred as it also affects foreign consumers, including tourists and daily cross-border commuters.
### The role of the November 29 vote [Discover how your AHV pension is calculated](nav:pension) with simulators dedicated to cross-border commuters. The popular vote on November 29 will be decisive. If the Swiss approve the AHV financing, the measure will come into effect according to the timetable set by the federal authorities. If the proposal is rejected, the Federal Parliament will have to find alternative solutions, potentially delaying the payment of the 13th pension.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ## What to do as a cross-border commuter
In this crucial phase, it is important to understand your current pension status and how the vote on November 29 could influence your financial future. Cross-border commuters have concrete tools at their disposal to plan ahead.
### Check your personal AVS statement
The first step is to ensure you have a complete contribution history with the Swiss AVS. You can request a free statement from the territorial compensation office in your canton of work. This document shows all recorded contributions over the years and estimates the future pension based on contributions made up to that point. It is essential to verify that no contribution year has been omitted by mistake, as any gap reduces the final pension.
### Pension planning across multiple pillars
While awaiting the referendum result, cross-border commuters can plan their pension future by considering the second pillar (LPP - Swiss pension fund) and the third pillar (3a). These components are independent of the AVS and provide crucial additional protection. Many cross-border commuters do not fully utilize the contribution possibilities of the third pillar, which offers tax advantages both in Switzerland and Italy through the Italian tax credit.
The third pillar allows for tax-deductible annual contributions: a long-term strategy that protects against regulatory uncertainties such as those surrounding AVS funding.
### Timeline of next steps
The vote is scheduled for November 29. Cross-border commuters will receive official information from their canton of work and the municipalities of residence in Italy. In the event of approval, the VAT increase will come into effect according to the details communicated by the federal authorities. In the event of rejection, the debate on AVS funding will continue in the federal and cantonal parliamentary bodies.
### Available digital tools
Use the [paycheck calculator](nav:calculator) to check the impact of various scenarios on your tax deductions and AVS contributions. With a [pension simulation tool](nav:pension), you can plan different pension scenarios considering possible changes in the funding system. These calculations will allow you to make informed decisions about contributions to the third pillar and your overall pension strategy.

item.description: Varese regional leader with +23% in exports. Switzerland is doing well (+21.2%), but the CIGS is growing (+14.9%), a sign of ongoing corporate reorganisations.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Varese export up by +23% in the first quarter of 2026. - Lombardy accounts for 25.2% of national export. - Export to Switzerland increases by 21.2%. - Regional CIGS grows by 14.9%.
- **What**: UIL Lombardia analysis of export and production. - When: First quarter of 2026. - Where: Province of Varese and Lombardy region. - Who: UIL Lombardia, coordinator Massafra, Secretary Albrizio. - Amount: 40.9 billion euros total regional export.
The first quarter of 2026 marked a significant milestone for the economy of the province of Varese, which recorded a 23% growth in exports, outperforming even the territory of Milan and securing the first place in the Lombardy region. This detailed picture was provided by a recent study conducted by UIL Lombardia. The Varese coordinator of the union, Massafra, emphasized the strategic importance of reinvesting these revenues in training, skills, safety, and stable work to consolidate the territorial leadership. However, the report highlights a complex situation: the increase in the use of the CIGS indicates that the growth in foreign sales does not guarantee uniform protection for all workers.
### The regional economic picture Lombardy confirms itself as the productive engine of Italy, producing alone 25.2% of the entire national export. The manufacturing sector remains the fundamental pillar, representing 97% of regional exports. Despite a hold on overall average values, the UIL analysis reveals deep territorial divisions and a significant increase in extraordinary unemployment benefits. The Secretary General of UIL Lombardia, Antonio Albrizio, specifies that, although not in a declared recessionary phase, the region faces strong pressures on production costs and a deterioration of corporate expectations. The need for a preventive and selective industrial policy therefore becomes a central theme for economic stability. The overall regional export exceeded 40.9 billion euros, marking a 0% annual variation and a -6.5% quarterly variation, while imports stood at 42.8 billion euros, with a negative trade balance of approximately 1.9 billion euros. The sectoral and geographical analysis conducted by UIL Lombardia, illustrated by the Confederation Secretary Vittorio Sarti, highlights heterogeneous market dynamics. A marked polarization in performance is observed: while the transport and pharmaceutical sectors grow by 12.1% and 9.7% respectively, other sectors show a significant slowdown. In particular, the textile-clothing-leather sector declines by 7.9%, chemicals by 6.1%, and the machinery sector records a decrease of 5.5%. These data reflect a production system in a phase of transformation, where employment stability is tested by corporate crises and structural reorganizations. A particularly interesting figure concerns commercial routes. Exports to Switzerland have increased by 21.2%, contrasting with the decline in sales to the United States, down by 4.4%, and a modest growth towards the European Union, at 1.0%. This export scenario to the Swiss Confederation assumes a significant role considering the large number of cross-border workers employed in Varese and Lombardy companies that maintain constant exchanges with the Swiss market. The link between commercial performance and personnel management clearly emerges from the data on wage guarantees. While total CIG decreases by 14.4% and CIGO (ordinary) shows a decrease of 26.2%, there is a worrying increase of 14.9% in CIGS (extraordinary). The latter is closely related to corporate reorganization processes, structural crises, and the use of solidarity contracts. It is evident that the distance between the performances of the twelve Lombard provinces, where only six show an increase in exports, confirms that the regional average cannot be the only parameter for defining employment support policies or crisis management. For those operating in corporate contexts subject to these fluctuations, it is essential to monitor not only sales volumes but also the use of social safety nets, which often represent the first sign of a change in production structures and, consequently, in the stability of the employment relationship.

In the summer of 1911, miners and steelmakers crossed their arms for months. Workers from other parts of Italy came to their aid. Including Gallarate, with the combative figure of the trade unionist Ines Oddone Bittelli. In August 1911, a group of children from the area of Piombino and Elba arrived in Gallarate. It is not a holiday of pleasure (tourism, for the most part, does not yet exist) but a temporary and necessary migration: children of striking workers are welcomed in Gallarate as a form of help to their families who are struggling. Leading the arrival of the little Tuscans in and around Gallarate was Ines Oddone, a determined trade unionist, journalist on 'The class struggle', champion of women's and children's rights, wife of the secretary of the Chamber of Labour Giovanni Bitelli. The foster care of the 'children of the serrati' will involve about two hundred children. From the beginning, the operation was conceived not only as a direct solidarity, but also as a political gesture: 'The children's exodus is at the same time a living message of love and hatred that comes to us from the countries in struggle and reminds us of the pact of the proletarian organization, the promises freely exchanged by our Leagues, the ultimate goal towards which the efforts of workers around the world tend,' writes Ines Oddone. The reception of the children of striking workers in Gallarate represents an example of class solidarity that today may seem incredible. Ines Oddone Bittelli, a unionist and journalist, was a key figure in this operation. Her determination and commitment to the rights of women and children were fundamental to the organization of the mass foster care of the children. Together with other unionists from Emilia-Romagna, Oddone organized the transfer of the children from Piombino to various Italian cities, including Gallarate.

item.description: The Joint Commission approved the Resolution on differentiated autonomy for Lombardy, with significant implications for frontier workers.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - The Joint Commission has approved the Resolution on differentiated autonomy. - The Resolution concerns health, civil protection, professions, and social security. - The Regional Council will continue the negotiation process with the State.
## Key facts - **What**: Approval of the Resolution on differentiated autonomy. - When: September 2, 2026. - Where: Palazzo Pirelli, Milan. - Who: Special Commission “Autonomy and reorganization of local autonomies” and Commission for Institutional Affairs and Local Entities. - Amount: Not specified.
The Special Commission “Autonomy and reorganization of local autonomies” and the Commission for Institutional Affairs and Local Entities held a joint session at Palazzo Pirelli on September 2, 2026, to vote on the Resolution on differentiated autonomy. The Resolution, approved by a majority, mandates the Regional Council to continue the negotiation process with the State. The texts at the center of the vote concern the final agreement frameworks agreed with the Government, namely the attribution of additional competences and functions to the Lombardy Region in non-LEP matters (“civil protection”, “professions”, “complementary and supplementary social security”) and in the matter of “health protection – coordination of public finance”.
### Reactions of the Presidents The President of the Special Commission on Autonomy, Giovanni Malanchini (Lega), stated: “I am very satisfied with a process that has lasted three and a half years and will see its concluding act next week with the final vote in the Assembly. Regardless of all political positions, I want to thank all the commissioners for the relationship of loyal and correct collaboration that has characterized these years. Our work has always been based on total transparency and openness to dialogue with the minorities, carving out for the Commission a role entirely independent and autonomous from the Council, guaranteeing and protecting the centrality of the Regional Council. Thanks to this process, we arrive at a framework of functions that will allow Lombardy to respond with greater promptness, efficiency, and subsidiarity to the needs of citizens and businesses.”
The President of the Commission for Institutional Affairs, Matteo Forte (FdI), shared the same view, emphasizing the significance of the approved directive: “We are facing an important moment that is the outcome of solid work but represents a starting point and not an end. Differentiated autonomy is a dynamic process: with this Resolution, we give a clear mandate to the Council to continue the dialogue on further competences. What we approve is a necessary tool to ensure greater proximity of institutions to the needs of the territories.”
During today’s session, an amendment presented by Councilor Onorio Rosati (AVS) was put to a vote and rejected by a majority. The amendment requested that “the contents of the 2024 Constitutional Court ruling No. 192 be sufficiently valued in the text of the Resolution, fully incorporating what is contained in the premises of the preintese between the Lombardy Region and the Government.”
A negative vote was also cast for the popular petition promoted by some associations (from the Associations Coordinamento per la Democrazia Costituzionale – Milan, Libertà e Giustizia – Milan Circle and Comitati per il ritiro di ogni autonomia differenziata – Lombardy) which had collected, by the end of 2025, through the online platform Open Petition, the signatures of over 1500 citizens and asked the regional representatives to interrupt the process on differentiated autonomy.
From the opposition benches, numerous Councilors intervened: Carlo Borghetti (PD), Emilio Del Bono (PD), Gian Mario Fragomeli (PD), Michela Palestra (Patto Civico), and Onorio Rosati (AVS), all agreeing on their opposition to the Resolution.
“This is an act of grave political and procedural coercion that completely empties the sovereignty and guiding role of the Regional Council,” commented the minority representatives. “It is unacceptable that the Council has reactivated the dialogue with the Government based on an act from 2017 that is now completely outdated after the Constitutional Court ruling and the reduction of competences from 23 to just 4 matters. The choice was made to accelerate unjustifiably without prior debate in the Assembly of this legislature, ignoring the obligation of a rigorous investigation and bypassing a true preventive involvement of local entities, which risk having to manage... The approval of the Resolution has significant implications for commuters who work in Lombardy and reside in Ticino. The greater regional autonomy could lead to changes in health policies, civil protection, and professions, which could directly affect the daily lives of commuters. For example, greater regional control over health policies could result in more efficient management of resources and better quality of services provided, also benefiting commuters who use the Lombard health system.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). For cross-border workers who wish to delve into the implications of the Resolution on differentiated autonomy, it is important to follow some concrete actions. First of all, it is essential to stay updated on the new regional policies and the requirements to access the services offered by the Lombardy Region. Cross-border workers can consult the official website of the Lombardy Region to obtain updated and detailed information.

item.title: AVS-INPS 2026 coordination: family with children
item.description: Total AVS-INPS contributions for border workers with children: how to coordinate the pension between Switzerland and Italy by 2026.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - AVS-INPS coordination is essential for cross-border workers with family - New Cross-Border Agreement from 1 January 2024 changes taxation - Totalization of contributions: joint counting of AVS-INPS - Family with children has rights to LAMal and specific benefits
## Key facts - **What**: Coordination between Swiss AVS and Italian INPS - When: Effective from 1 January 2024 - Where: Swiss-Italian border - Who: SECO, Canton Ticino and INPS - Agreement: Signed on 23 December 2020, effective 1 January 2024 - Regimes: Old cross-border workers exemption €7'500 (transitional 2024-2033), new €10'000 - LAMal: Franchises CHF 300-2500 adults, right of option group G - Tax: Withheld ONLY in Switzerland, no double taxation
On 1 January 2024, the New Cross-Border Agreement between Switzerland and Italy, signed on 23 December 2020, came into force. This agreement introduces automatic coordination between the AVS (Swiss old-age insurance) and INPS (Italian pension institute) systems, allowing cross-border workers to totalize the contributions paid in both countries. For those working in Ticino as cross-border workers and have children, this novelty completely transforms pension planning and family rights.
Before this reform, coordinating a pension between Switzerland and Italy required lengthy calculations and administrative negotiations. The new automatic regime eliminates much of this complexity. However, the reform clearly distinguishes between two categories of cross-border workers: those already registered before 17 July 2023 access a transitional regime with an exemption of €7'500 until 31 December 2033, while new cross-border workers have a franchise of €10'000. To understand which regime applies to you, you can quickly verify your rights and cross-border status.
### AVS-INPS coordination: how totalization works
Totalization means that contributions paid in one country are also counted for the other pension system when calculating the old-age pension. Concretely: a cross-border worker who has worked 25 years in Switzerland and 10 in Italy will not have to wait for the completion of Italian contributions to receive the Swiss AVS pension. The two systems coordinate and ensure joint counting, avoiding the loss of contributions due to a change in the country of work.
Withholding tax on employment income remains a Swiss competence. The cross-border worker receives tax withholdings only in Switzerland, not in double taxation. Italy avoids duplication through the tax credit (CE box of the Italian 730 declaration). This mechanism is governed by the Italian-Swiss Convention on double taxation, signed on 9 December 1976, and ensures that taxes are not paid on the same income in both countries.
For cross-border workers with family, 2024 has brought further clarifications on rights related to children: tax deductions, family allowances where applicable, parental leave, and LAMal coverage. LAMal (Swiss compulsory health insurance) recognizes the right of option for cross-border workers of group G: they can remain in the Italian system or join the Swiss system with franchises between CHF 300 and CHF 2500 for adults. The decision to coordinate the pension between AVS and INPS is not automatic: it requires awareness and active planning. A cross-border worker with children must evaluate which scenario is most advantageous. If they remain in Switzerland until retirement, AVS provides a solid base; if they plan to move to Italy before retirement, totalization with INPS becomes crucial. If they alternate periods between the two countries, automatic coordination offers protection. For a family with children, coordination has concrete implications for benefits. In Switzerland, the presence of children influences the contribution rates of the LPP (second pillar): those with children have lower savings rates in the 25-34 age bracket (7-10% instead of the standard 7-18%). The Italian INPS does not apply the same direct benefit, but offers family allowances if the cross-border worker remains registered in the Italian system. The choice of coordination does not cancel these benefits; rather, it preserves them through totalization. Scenario: a Ticino cross-border worker with 20 years of AVS contributions in Switzerland (starting at 25 years old) and 15 years of INPS contributions in Italy (after a temporary move). Without totalization, they would reach 35 years of AVS contributions by 60 years old but would not be entitled to a full Italian pension (which requires 20 years of contributions). With totalization from January 1, 2024, the 20 Swiss years are counted towards the Italian requirement, accelerating the right to the Italian pension and ensuring a coordinated pension from 65 years old. This protection also extends to the cross-border worker's children, who maintain continuous health coverage during the transition. The [LAMal in Switzerland](nav:health) offers tiered deductibles. A family with 2 children has different costs depending on the age bracket. If the children were born in Italy but reside in Ticino during the cross-border worker's employment, LAMal with the Swiss option ensures continuity. If the family resides in Italy but the cross-border worker works in Ticino, the Group G option right allows them to maintain Swiss LAMal for the children, provided they are part of the declared family unit.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). Planning the AVS-INPS coordination for a family with children requires a step-by-step procedure. The first step is to verify your status: having a valid Permit G and being registered with the cantonal employment office in Ticino. The Permit G is the necessary condition to access the benefits of coordination. Many commuters do not explicitly verify this, but it is crucial to check before starting any pension procedure. The second step involves contribution statements. Contact the SECO (State Secretariat for Economic Affairs) or the cantonal tax office in your Ticino canton to obtain a statement of AVS contributions paid to date. Simultaneously, consult the INPS website or contact a CAF (tax assistance center) in Italy to obtain the INPS contribution statement. These two documents are essential: they will provide an accurate picture of your coordinated pension rights. The third step is to obtain an estimate of the coordinated pension. Some commuters turn to specialized insurance brokers, others directly to the SECO or Ticino tax consultants. The important thing is to have a credible projection of what your AVS pension will be at 65 years coordinated with the INPS portion. Knowing this amount allows you to evaluate whether it is necessary to supplement with the Swiss third pillar (pillar 3a), which offers tax advantages and tax-free pensions in Switzerland. ### Operational checklist: 7 concrete steps - Verify valid Permit G with the cantonal office - Request AVS contribution statement from SECO or cantonal administration - Request INPS contribution statement via INPS website or CAF - Obtain coordinated pension estimate from broker or consultant - Evaluate LAMal option (Switzerland vs. Italy) for the family - Open a pillar 3a with a Swiss bank/insurance if convenient - Communicate data to both systems at least 1-2 years before retirement For those with children, coordination also impacts the tax return. Once the commuter reaches retirement age, the joint AVS-INPS declaration must reflect total contributions and minimum supplements. If the commuter has benefited from exemptions or allowances (€7,500 or €10,000 depending on whether they are an old or new commuter), these reductions apply only to the taxable income in Switzerland but do not cancel INPS rights. Use our [pension and paycheck calculator](nav:pension) to simulate different AVS-INPS coordination scenarios based on your current contributions. If you have children and want to understand how deductions and benefits change, you can also consult our [commuters tax calculation tools](nav:calculator) for an overview of your taxes, refunds, and family rights. Early planning 5-10 years before retirement is the best strategy to avoid leaving resources on the table.

item.description: The new 2024 cross-border agreement and the 2026 IRPEF rates make the exchange rate strategy critical. Practical guide for singles: timing, procedures, operational tools.
item.content:encoded:
## In short - New Cross-border Agreement in force from 1 January 2024: modified tax regime - IRPEF rates 2026: 23% up to €28,000, 35% up to €50,000, 43% above - Withholding tax ONLY in Switzerland; tax credit in Italy - Timing of the EUR-CHF exchange rate is critical for the real net of single cross-border workers
## Key facts - **What**: New cross-border agreement between Switzerland and Italy - When: Effective January 1, 2024 (signed December 23, 2020) - Where: Ticino-Italy cross-border workers (Brogeda, Gaggiolo, Ponte Tresa, Chiasso passes) - Who: SECO (Switzerland), INPS and Revenue Agency (Italy) - Regimes: Old cross-border commuters exemption €7,500 (transit 2024–2033); new €10,000 - Rates: Italian IRPEF 23%, 35%, 43% by bands; AVS/AI Switzerland 5.3% - Tax: Withheld ONLY in Switzerland; double taxation avoided with tax credit (EC framework of 730)
Starting from 1 January 2024, the New Cross-border Agreement between Switzerland and Italy has significantly changed the tax and contribution regime of those who work in Swiss territory and reside in Italy. For the single cross-border worker, this transition has concrete implications on the management of the CHF-EUR exchange rate: the real net varies not only with the volatility of the currency pair, but also with the tax declaration deadlines and the timing of conversion of the salary into euros.
The withholding tax remains withheld exclusively in Switzerland (AVS/AI 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF 0.7–1.5%, LPP 7–18% depending on the age group). In Italy, the IRPEF applied is the ordinary one: 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001 and €50,000, 43% over €50,000. The double payment does not occur because the Italian system recognizes a tax credit (EC framework of 730) which compensates for the Swiss withholding. Consequently, the single cross-border worker must plan when to convert the CHF into EUR based on the prevailing exchange rate, aware that the Italian tax authorities will reference a specific rate for the calculation of the tax base.
For cross-border workers who were already cross-border workers before 17 July 2023, a transitional regime has been envisaged: exemption of up to €7,500 per year, with gradual adjustment until 2033. For new cross-border workers, the exemption is €10,000.
### Withholding tax and currency conversion
The single cross-border worker receives his salary in CHF in his Swiss bank account and has discretion in converting to EUR. The withholding of AVS/AI (5.3%) and other contributions (AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF 0.7–1.5%) takes place directly from the paycheck in Switzerland, not in Italy. This means that the taxable amount declared to the Italian tax authorities is already gross of these Swiss withholdings. Subsequently, in Italy, the tax credit (EC framework of 730) subtracts the taxes paid in Switzerland from the tax base, avoiding penalties. The timing of the exchange rate - i.e. the moment in which to convert CHF to EUR - affects the real purchasing power in Italy, not on taxation per se, but on how much euro the cross-border worker actually receives for daily expenses. ### EUR-CHF volatility: the silent impact on the net
The Convention between Italy and Switzerland, signed on 9 December 1976, establishes that the main tax burden remains with the country where the income is produced (Switzerland for our cross-border workers). However, the Italian tax credit mechanism presupposes that the cross-border worker declares his income in EUR, applying a reference exchange rate. If the cross-border worker changes his CHF into EUR at a worse rate (e.g. 1.00 CHF = 0.95 EUR) than the declaration rate (e.g. 1.00 CHF = 1.05 EUR), he loses the difference, even if the tax remains formally correct.
Let's consider a hypothetical scenario: a single cross-border worker earns 80,000 CHF gross per year in Switzerland, to which AVS/AI (5.3%), AD/AC (1.1%), LAINF (0.7%) and LPP (7–18% depending on age, let's assume 10%) apply. The total Swiss withholding tax is approximately 24.1%, leaving a net of ~CHF60,720. If the cross-border worker converts at the rate of 1.00 CHF = 0.95 EUR, he receives ~57,684 EUR. However, if the average reporting rate for IRPEF is 1.00 CHF = 1.02 EUR, the Italian tax authorities tax it on 81,600 EUR (80,000 * 1.02), not on 57,684. This creates a discrepancy that the single cross-border worker must manage when filling out the 730, because the Revenue Agency compares the theoretical IRPEF (out of EUR 81,600) with the Swiss taxes paid (already counted in CHF converted at the declaration rate), and if the result is negative, it issues a refund.
### Timing and exchange strategy
For the single cross-border worker who has discretion over the conversion timing, there are three approaches:
- **Passive strategy**: convert monthly at a fixed rate (reduces the concentrated risk of a bad rate, moving average of the exchange rate) - Active strategy: monitor historical EUR-CHF volatility bands (usually 0.92–1.08) and convert when the pair is favorable - Institutional instruments: Swiss banks (PostFinance, Raiffeisen, UBS) offer cross-border accounts with competitive rates compared to online money transfers
KVG, the Swiss health insurance (adult deductible CHF 300–2,500), remains paid in CHF. For the single cross-border worker, this is an additional consideration: part of the Swiss net must remain in francs to cover this mandatory expense, limiting the amount available for conversion and transfer to Italy. The conversion window therefore begins after having set aside the amount for KVG and other expenses in Swiss territory. ### Practical checklist for single cross-border commuters in 2026
Step 1: Check your border status - Are you an 'old cross-border worker' (already one before 17 July 2023)? Benefit from the €7,500 exemption until 2033. - Are you a 'new cross-border worker'? The deductible is €10,000. - Verify that you have the G Permit at the SEM (Secretariat of State for Migration).
Step 2: Collect the documents for the 730 - Swiss bank statements (gross CHF, details of AVS/AI/AD/AC/LAINF/LPP withholdings). - Swiss employer's certificate (income summary document). - Print certificate of withholding tax paid in Switzerland (to be requested from AFC/ESTV, Cantonal Federal Tax Administration).
Step 3: Determine the declarative exchange rate The exchange rate for IRPEF is established by the Revenue Agency and published monthly. It does not coincide with the bank rate on the day of your conversion. Calculate your income in EUR using the Agency rate, valid in the month in which you received the income. Consult the Revenue Agency website > foreign section > exchange rates.
Step 4: Fill in the 730 CE form In the CE framework (foreign income), declare the gross income in EUR (converted at the Agency rate), the taxes paid in Switzerland, and request the tax credit. The Agency will compare the IRPEF you should pay in Italy with the Swiss taxes paid; will return the difference (if in your favor) to you by refund by November–December 2026.
Step 5: Manage currency exchange strategically - Open a current account with a Swiss bank (PostFinance, Raiffeisen) that offers competitive rates for cross-border commuters. - Program monthly conversions or according to volatility: do not convert everything at once to avoid concentrated negative rate risk. - Monitor online exchange platforms (Wise, OFX) and compare with traditional banks before each transaction.
**Step 6: Deadlines 2026** - Declare to the SEM any change in situation (new employer, move, termination of employment). - Submit the 730 by 30 September 2026 (ordinary deadline) through your CAF or accountant. - If you are entitled to refunds, these are generally credited between November and December 2026 by the Revenue Agency.
### Tools and resources to learn more
Use Frontaliere Ticino's [calcolatore di stipendio frontaliere](nav:calculator) to simulate your monthly net in different exchange rate scenarios. Also consult the guide on [dichiarazione dei redditi frontalieri](nav:tax-return) and [comparatore di banche frontaliere](nav:banks) to identify the account with the best conditions for exchange and liquidity management in two currencies.
Contact SECO for clarifications on the G Permit and AFC/ESTV for details on Swiss contribution rates. In Italy, the Revenue Agency provides assistance services on completing the 730 for cross-border workers; the declarative exchange rate is published monthly on the official website. To monitor EUR-CHF volatility in real time, consult financial sites such as XE.com, OANDA, or Bloomberg that offer charts and histories of the currency pair.

item.title: Border tax credit 2026: calculation with children
item.description: How to recover excess taxes in Italy: the practical guide for border workers with children, from the calculation of the deductible to the use of the 730 model.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Tax credit recoverable via 730 from January 1, 2024 - Exemption €7,500 (pre-2023 commuters), €10,000 (new) - Tax withheld only in Switzerland, compensated in Italy - Family with children: increased exemption
## Key facts - **What**: Tax credit for double taxation Switzerland-Italy - When: Effective from January 1, 2024 (New Cross-Border Workers Agreement) - Where: Cross-border workers residing in Italy, working in Switzerland - Who: INPS and Agenzia delle Entrate manage the mechanism - Exemption: €7,500 (previous cross-border workers transitional regime 2024–2033) - New exemption: €10,000 for new cross-border workers
The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement, signed on December 23, 2020 and effective from January 1, 2024, has transformed the tax system for those working in Switzerland and residing in Italy. Before this date, the regime was significantly different; today cross-border workers benefit from a tax credit in the CE section of the Italian declaration, compensating for the taxes withheld at source by the Swiss employer.
For cross-border workers who have a family with children, the implications are significant. The withholding tax is levied exclusively in Switzerland (not in both countries), and the recovery occurs through the Italian 730 model by attaching Swiss documentation. The exemption, i.e., the amount of tax-free income, depends on the status: cross-border workers who were already such before July 17, 2023, benefit from an exemption of €7,500, applicable in the transitional regime covering the years 2024–2033. New cross-border workers, on the other hand, are entitled to an exemption of €10,000.
### Calculation of double taxation The calculation mechanism is based on the Italy-Switzerland Double Taxation Convention (signed on December 9, 1976), which establishes when one State has the right to tax the income. In the case of cross-border workers, Switzerland applies the withholding tax rate (single taxation), and Italy recognizes the credit through the 730, avoiding double taxation. For a family with children, the Swiss pay slips already report the withholding calculated according to the applicable federal and cantonal rates (for example, the Italian IRPEF could be 23% up to €28,000, 35% between €28,001–50,000, 43% over €50,000, but the Swiss withholding follows different criteria). It is essential to keep all Swiss documents (income source certificate, pay slips) to prove the tax paid in Switzerland during the compilation of the Italian declaration. ### Practical scenarios for a family with children Consider a couple of cross-border workers with a dependent child. If both work in Switzerland and live in bordering Italy, each applies their own allowance: those who were already cross-border workers before July 2023 benefit from €7,500, while newcomers benefit from €10,000 (if hired afterward). Swiss pay slips will record the withholding according to local rates (e.g., Canton Ticino or Graubünden), while Italy will recognize the credit in the CE section of the 730 declaration. The family's total income is the sum of individual incomes, net of Swiss withholding. In the Italian 730, each cross-border worker submits their own form with the certificate of taxable income from a foreign source (equivalent Swiss CUD) and calculates the credit as the difference between the Italian tax due and that already paid at source in Switzerland. If the Swiss withholding exceeds the Italian tax due for that income bracket, the credit is positive and generates a refund (rebate). If the withholding is lower, the cross-border worker will have to complete the payment in Italy. For a family with children, the situation may change: the allowance increases if the spouse also has cross-border worker status, and deductions for dependent children (if resident in Italy) are applied in the Italian declaration. It is necessary to verify whether the children have been declared in the Swiss pay slip (with corresponding Swiss deductions) or if they are only declared in Italy: this influences the final calculation. ### Required documentation To complete the 730 and claim the credit, the cross-border worker must provide: - Certificate of income from a Swiss source (equivalent to CUD, issued by the Swiss employer or the Swiss database) - Copy of the final pay slip of the year (to verify withholdings) - [Work permit (Permit G)](nav:permits) and proof of residence in Italy - If necessary, the Swiss declaration sent to the Swiss tax administration (not mandatory for many cross-border workers if the withholding is final, but useful as proof) Filling out the CE section of the Italian declaration requires attention: the income must be declared gross of Swiss withholding, the credit must be calculated accurately, and supporting documentation must be attached. A common mistake is confusing the withholding at source with the credit: the former is the amount withheld in the pay slip (already paid in Switzerland), the latter is the recognition in Italy of that taxation. ### Step-by-step procedure for tax credit recovery The process begins during the working year: the cross-border worker regularly receives Swiss pay slips, which show the withholding tax. At the end of the working year, they request the income certificate from the Swiss employer or download it from the Federal Tax Administration (FTA) portal. This document is essential as it shows the gross annual income and the total tax paid at source.
Next, the cross-border worker completes the [Italian 730 form](nav:tax-return) (or relies on a tax intermediary). In section CE (foreign income), they enter the income declared in Switzerland before withholding tax, specify the foreign country (Switzerland), and calculate the credit using the formula: credit = (Italian tax due on foreign income) – (tax already paid in Switzerland). If the family's total income is included in the Swiss pay slips and there are no other Italian income sources, the 730 will be the only declaration tool in Italy.
Once the 730 is submitted (through a tax intermediary, online via the Revenue Agency portal, or at the CAF/patronato), the Agency processes the declaration. If the credit exceeds the tax due, the cross-border worker is entitled to a refund. If it is lower, they must pay the difference. Refund times vary, but they are generally credited within a few months of submission and subsequent formal review.
### Deadlines and checklist The main deadlines are: - **By February 28** (or the next legal deadline): submission of the 730 to the Revenue Agency - Throughout the year: keep all Swiss pay slips and documentation related to dependents to supplement the Italian declaration - G permit: ensure it is valid for the entire tax year (the credit is valid only if the cross-border worker was regularly employed and resident)
Operational checklist for cross-border workers with children: - [ ] Request the income certificate from the Swiss employer - [ ] Collect all pay slips of the year (original or digital) - [ ] Verify status (old or new cross-border worker) to apply the correct exemption - [ ] Document dependents and their country of residence (Italy or Switzerland) - [ ] If the spouse is also a cross-border worker, collect the spouse's income documentation - [ ] Complete the 730 or delegate to a tax intermediary (CAF, accountant) - [ ] Attach the Swiss certificate and copies of pay slips to the 730 - [ ] Submit by the February deadline - [ ] Monitor the refund in the restricted area of the Revenue Agency
To simplify this process and estimate the expected withholding tax, a [pay slip calculator](nav:calculator) allows you to verify the tax credit amount before submitting the 730.

item.description: Calculate the Swiss net 2026: AVS rates 5.3%, tax at source, New Agreement, exemptions €7,500-€10,000 and Italian tax credit.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Withholding tax only in Switzerland: no double taxation thanks to the Italian tax credit - New Agreement 2024: old cross-border workers exemption €7,500, new €10,000 - Mandatory rates: AVS 5.3%, AD/AC 1.1%, LAINF 0.7-1.5%, LPP 7-18% per age bracket
## Key facts - **What**: Swiss payslip with AVS, AD/AC, LAINF, LPP deductions and withholding tax - When: Calculations 2026 according to the New Cross-Border Workers Agreement (effective 1 January 2024) - Where: Cross-border workers Italy-Switzerland, Canton Ticino - Who: Cross-border workers employed in Switzerland with permit G - Tax: Withheld only in Switzerland, tax credit in Italy (CE 730 form) - Exemption: Old cross-border workers €7,500, new €10,000 annually
The Swiss payslip of the cross-border worker is not a simple subtraction of gross minus net. It is the intertwining of five levels of mandatory deductions that add up before generating the Swiss taxable income: AVS/AI/IPG at 5.3%, AD/AC at 1.1%, LAINF between 0.7% and 1.5%, LPP from 7% to 18% depending on the age bracket (from 25 years onwards), and finally the federal and cantonal withholding tax. Each item has its own logic, but the biggest surprise is often the withholding tax: it is withheld directly in Switzerland, without Italy applying an additional tax. The mechanism is the tax credit provided by the CE section of the Italian income tax return, a protection that dates back to the Double Taxation Convention signed on 9 December 1976 between Italy and Switzerland.
The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement, signed on 23 December 2020 and entered into force on 1 January 2024 (Italian Law 83 of 13 June 2023), has brought a paradigm shift: cross-border workers already registered before 17 July 2023 (the "old" ones) benefit from an annual exemption of €7,500 in the transitional regime 2024–2033, while "new" cross-border workers obtain a franchise of €10,000. Both exemptions are deducted from the Italian taxable income before applying the IRPEF.
### Anatomy of the Swiss payslip
The structure of the Swiss payslip follows a rigid and transparent scheme. The contractual gross is the starting point; from there, the employer applies the mandatory social contributions in cascade. The AVS/AI/IPG (social security and disability) absorbs 5.3% of the salary. The AD/AC (unemployment and competitiveness insurance) cuts 1.1%, with a maximum cap of CHF 148,200 of taxable income. The LAINF (workplace accidents) varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the sector and risk class. The LPP (second pillar pension fund) depends on the worker's age: between 25 and 34 years it is about 7%, and grows up to 18% for those closest to retirement. After these four items, a reduced gross subtotal is calculated (gross minus all contributions). The withholding tax falls on this subtotal, which varies by canton, municipality, and personal rate. On average, the gross-net tax burden is between 15% and 17% of the initial salary. ## New Agreement: the change of rules for old and new cross-border workers
The New Cross-Border Workers Agreement has introduced two parallel and time-limited regimes. "Old" cross-border workers — i.e., those who already had cross-border worker status before July 17, 2023 — enjoy an Italian tax exemption of €7,500 annually starting from January 1, 2024, and until December 31, 2033. This is a ten-year exemption designed to facilitate the transition to a new system. "New" cross-border workers — hired as cross-border workers after July 17, 2023 — are entitled to an annual allowance of €10,000, with no time limit.
How does this apply in practice? A cross-border worker with a gross Swiss salary of 60,000 CHF first incurs Swiss deductions (AVS 5.3% = CHF 3,180, AD/AC 1.1% = CHF 660, LAINF 1% = CHF 600, LPP 7% average = CHF 4,200), totaling approximately CHF 8,640. This leaves a gross Swiss salary of CHF 51,360. The federal, cantonal, and communal withholding tax varies, but assuming an average burden of 16%, it absorbs an additional CHF 8,200. The Swiss net salary drops to CHF 43,160.
This net salary, converted to euros at the exchange rate of the tax year (let's say 1 CHF = 1.05 EUR for simplicity), becomes approximately €43,320. In Italy, the cross-border worker declares the gross Swiss income in the CE section of the 730 form: it is €63,000 (60,000 CHF ÷ 0.952 for the average exchange rate). If they are an "old" cross-border worker, they subtract €7,500, bringing the taxable amount to €55,500. The Italian IRPEF (23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% over €50,000) would generate a theoretical tax of €28,000 × 0.23 + €22,500 × 0.35 = €6,440 + €7,875 = €14,315. But on the declaration, Italy recognizes the Swiss tax credit: the withholding tax paid in Switzerland (CHF 8,200 ≈ €7,790) is subtracted. The result: the cross-border worker must pay approximately €4,525 additionally, or if the Swiss tax is higher than the presumed Italian IRPEF, they receive a refund.
### The role of the tax credit and double taxation
The Italy-Switzerland Double Taxation Convention of December 9, 1976 established a cornerstone principle: taxation occurs in the country where the economic activity is carried out (Switzerland, where the employer is based). Italy does not impose a separate second tax on foreign income; instead, it applies a tax credit (CE section of the 730 form). This credit is compensation for taxes paid abroad: if the Swiss rates are higher than the presumed Italian IRPEF, the credit covers the entire difference (and sometimes generates an Italian refund). If the Swiss rates are lower, Italy requires the balance.
The advantage of the credit is twofold: first, it avoids legal double taxation (paying taxes in both countries on the same income); second, it protects the cross-border worker from currency fluctuations and changes in rates. If the CHF weakens and the nominal Swiss tax remains the same but its value in EUR decreases, the Italian credit can still cover the lower amount, without penalties.
## Useful tools for your case To verify your within/over 20 km tax scenario, use the [net salary calculator](nav:calculator) and the [tax return guide](nav:tax-return). ## Step by step: how to calculate the net 2026
Calculating the real net of a Swiss payslip requires systematicity. Here is the procedure.
Step 1: collect the gross contractual amount Start from the value declared in the Swiss employment contract. There are no surprises here: if the contract says 60,000 CHF per year, the gross is 60,000 CHF. You will divide by 12 or 13 if you are paid monthly or for 13 months.
Step 2: subtract the mandatory social contributions Apply the rates: - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% of the gross - AD/AC: 1.1% of the gross (up to a ceiling of CHF 148,200 of taxable income) - LAINF: between 0.7% and 1.5% (variable by sector; consult your employer or the labor office) - LPP: depends on age. From 25 years old, it starts at 7% and rises up to 18%. Your payslip will indicate the exact percentage for your age group.
The subtotal of these four items represents 15–18% of the initial gross. Example: 60,000 CHF × 14.5% (average) = CHF 8,700. Remaining CHF 51,300.
Step 3: estimate the withholding tax The federal, cantonal, and municipal tax varies for the canton of Ticino and for the place of residence / work. The average burden in Ticino is between 14% and 17% of the subtotal after contributions. On CHF 51,300: between CHF 7,182 and CHF 8,721. Subtract this amount from the subtotal. Estimated Swiss net: between CHF 42,579 and CHF 44,118.
Step 4: record the income in the Italian declaration and apply the tax credit The gross Swiss income (60,000 CHF) is entered in the CE section of the Italian model 730. Convert using the exchange rate of the tax year (for 2026, use the average ISTAT exchange rate or the one published by the Revenue Agency). If you are an "old" cross-border worker, subtract €7,500 from the Italian taxable income; if you are "new," subtract €10,000. Calculate the theoretical Italian IRPEF (23% up to €28,000, 35% from €28,001 to €50,000, 43% beyond). Then, apply the tax credit: the sum of the Swiss withholding tax (converted into euros) becomes a credit against the Italian IRPEF. If the credit is higher than the theoretical IRPEF, you receive a refund; if lower, you pay the balance.
### Operational checklist for 2026
☐ Collect all Swiss payslips of the year (paper copies or PDF from the LPA, the employer's online payroll platform) ☐ Personally verify the AVS, AD/AC, LAINF, LPP rates in the payslip (they are not standardized: they vary by canton, employer, age, and sector) ☐ Calculate the Swiss gross-net using an Excel sheet or the [payslip simulator](nav:payslip) of the site ☐ Convert the gross Swiss income into EUR using the average exchange rate of the tax year (available at the Revenue Agency) ☐ Prepare the CE section of the Italian model 730 with: foreign gross income (in EUR), tax paid abroad (in EUR), exemption €7,500 (old) or €10,000 (new) ☐ Calculate the theoretical Italian IRPEF (apply the 23%-35%-43% rates) ☐ Subtract the tax credit from the theoretical IRPEF ☐ If the balance is negative, you are entitled to a refund; if positive, you must pay it ☐ Use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) of the site for quick scenarios and comparisons ☐ Entrust the final calculation of the declaration to a tax consultant specialized in cross-border workers, especially if your situation includes multiple sources of income, a spouse declared as a dependent, or changes in permit during the year
Practical simulation shows that the real net of a 2026 cross-border worker depends on three mobile factors: the Swiss cantonal rate (which varies by place of work and residence), the CHF-EUR exchange rate, and the Italian tax exemption regime (€7,500 or €10,000). A Ticino tax consultant with transnational experience can adapt these calculations to your specific situation and ensure compliance with both tax systems (Swiss and Italian). For an initial and quick estimate, use the [salary calculator](nav:calculator) available on the site.

item.description: From the New Frontier Agreement in force since 2024: how to calculate the AVS, LPP, LAMal withholdings and the tax at source in the Swiss paycheck.
item.content:encoded:
## In brief - Withholding tax only in Switzerland from 1 January 2024 - Exemption €7,500 (old cross-border workers) or €10,000 (new cross-border workers) - AVS/AI/IPG 5.3%, LPP 7-18%, LAMal optional for Permit G
## Key facts - **What**: New payroll rules for Italian cross-border workers - When: 1 January 2024 (New Cross-Border Agreement in force) - Where: Switzerland (all cantons) - Who: Italian cross-border workers with Permit G/B - Old exemption: €7,500 annually (transitional regime 2024–2033) - New exemption: €10,000 annually - AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% of gross salary (employee)
The New Cross-Border Agreement, signed on 23 December 2020 and effective from 1 January 2024, has redesigned the payroll rules for Italian cross-border workers in Switzerland. One of the most relevant novelties concerns the withholding tax regime, now exclusively withheld in Switzerland and never in Italy. The paradigm shift to avoid double taxation passes through the new exemption, which varies depending on whether you are an 'old cross-border worker' (already such before 17 July 2023) or a 'new cross-border worker' who entered after that date.
The Italian ratification of the agreement took place through Law No. 83 of 13 June 2023. For old cross-border workers, the transitional regime provides an exemption of €7,500 gross per year, with the right to tax credit in the Italian 730 model. New cross-border workers, on the other hand, benefit from a franchise of €10,000. In the transitional regime from 2024 to 2033, the amount subject to withholding tax varies depending on the year, until the distinction between the two categories ceases.
The Convention against Double Taxation Italy-Switzerland (signed on 9 December 1976) remains the legal foundation for the tax credit that cross-border workers report in the CE section of the 730. Italy, in fact, does not apply income tax to the work of those who work in Switzerland — because Switzerland is not a member of the EU/EEA and has its own tax regime. The withholding therefore takes place only once, with the Swiss employer, eliminating the risk of double taxation.
### Composition of mandatory withholdings in the pay slip
Understanding the composition of the pay slip is the first step to verify that the withholdings are correct. The main mandatory contributions that you will see in the pay slip are AVS (old-age and disability insurance), AI (disability), IPG (loss of earnings allowance) — together withheld at 5.3% of the gross — and the LAMal fund (health insurance) which, unlike AVS/AI/IPG, is optional for cross-border workers with Permit G, although it remains an essential coverage. [Discover which contributions a LAMal coverage entails and which deductible to choose](nav:health).
In addition to employee contributions, the pay slip shows AD (unemployment insurance) and AC (insolvency compensation), both at 1.1% (with a maximum of CHF 148,200 of insured salary) and LAINF (accident insurance), which varies between 0.7% and 1.5% depending on the risk of the activity. The employer also pays their share of contributions (not directly visible in the pay slip, but still a company expense).
Finally, there is the LPP (second pillar pension fund), with contribution rates ranging from 7% to 18% depending on the age group, starting from 25 years. This age differentiation reflects the risk profile and the number of years until retirement. ### How the net salary is composed
The net salary that a cross-border worker receives each month is the result of a methodical subtraction between the agreed gross salary and a series of mandatory deductions. In the case of Italian cross-border workers, the calculation is complicated by the two different withholding tax rates applied depending on whether the worker is a "old" or "new" cross-border worker.
Let's take a generic scenario: a cross-border worker receives an agreed gross salary (Bruttolohn in Swiss German). From this amount, the following deductions are made, in order:
1. AVS/AI/IPG: 5.3% of the gross, withheld as a mandatory contribution for social benefits. 2. AD/AC: 1.1% up to a maximum of CHF 148,200 of insured income per year. 3. LAINF: 0.7-1.5% depending on the sector of activity. 4. LPP: 7-18% depending on age (from 25 years onwards). 5. LAMal: Optional for Permit G. If joined, approximately 5-8% of the gross is withheld (but varies based on the premium and deductible, generally CHF 300–2,500 for adults). 6. Withholding tax: Now withheld only in Switzerland. The first amount (€7,500 for old, €10,000 for new) remains tax-free.
### Old vs new cross-border workers: the impact on the paycheck
The distinction between those who were already cross-border workers before July 17, 2023, and those who entered afterward is not merely academic—it has direct implications for the monthly paycheck and the annual tax return.
**Old cross-border workers**: Benefit from an exemption of €7,500 per year in the transitional regime that develops from 2024 to 2033. During the transitional regime, the amount subject to withholding tax varies year by year, allowing a gradual adjustment to the new system.
New cross-border workers: Enjoy a fixed exemption of €10,000 per year, without reductions. This greater protection reflects the intention to attract new cross-border labor to the Swiss market.
In both cases, the tax-free amount translates into a slightly more advantageous monthly paycheck and, above all, a lower amount to be declared in the Italian 730 tax return. The tax credit in the CE section of the 730 covers the Swiss withholding tax paid, eliminating double payment.
### Deadlines and tax return procedure
Each month, the Swiss employer delivers the paycheck to the cross-border worker (in German/French depending on the canton). The Italian tax return is made by November 30 of the following year using the 730 form, filled out at a CAF or accountant. In the CE section, the taxes paid at source in Switzerland must be indicated to obtain the tax credit. [Read the guide on declaring Swiss income](nav:tax-return) to correctly integrate the data in Italy.
It is essential to keep all annual paychecks and Swiss tax certificates (such as the employer's certificate reporting the gross and deductions), as the Italian Revenue Agency and the MEF may request them in case of checks. Switzerland does not automatically transmit tax data to Italy (since it is not a member of the EU/EEA), so the correct declaration depends on the cross-border worker.
## Useful planning tools To estimate your pension strategy, use the [pension planner](nav:pension) and the [pillar 3 simulator](nav:pillar3). ### Checklist: how to verify your payslip every month
Once you receive your payslip from your Swiss employer, the cross-border worker should follow a simple procedure to check that the calculations are correct:
1. Check the gross amount: Verify that the gross salary corresponds to the amount agreed in the contract. Any difference (increments, agreed increases, bonuses) must be documented.
2. Verify AVS/AI/IPG deductions: These should be 5.3% of the gross amount. If the gross amount is, for example, CHF 4,000, the AVS/AI/IPG deductions should be approximately CHF 212.
3. Check AD/AC: Approximately 1.1% up to the annual maximum of CHF 148,200. If the cross-border worker has not yet reached the annual maximum, the deduction appears; once exceeded, it disappears from subsequent payslips.
4. Verify LAINF: Depends on the sector (between 0.7% and 1.5%). Compare with previous payslips to ensure consistency.
5. Check LPP: Should vary between 7% and 18% depending on your age bracket (from 25 years old). If you are under 25, it should not be deducted.
6. Check withholding tax: If the annual gross income exceeds the exemption (€7,500 for old, €10,000 for new), the deduction starts on the income above.
7. Keep the payslip: Digitally archive (scan) all Swiss payslips and tax documents.
### Annual deadlines and available tools
By December 31 of each year, the Swiss employer issues the tax certificate (Lohnausweiskopie) which reports: - Annual gross salary - All social deductions - Withholding tax paid
In March-May of the following year, the cross-border worker completes the 730 form at a CAF or accountant, entering: - In section RA the employment income - In section CE the taxes paid at source in Switzerland for the tax credit
### How to reduce the risk of errors in the payslip
The Swiss payslip remains one of the most important documents in the life of the cross-border worker. Understanding each element allows you to avoid surprises, verify the correct payment of contributions, and prepare calmly for the annual tax return. If you notice discrepancies, contact your Swiss employer and your Italian accountant promptly to avoid future disputes. [You can use our payslip calculator to simulate the net monthly amount and check the impact of deductions on your specific contract](nav:calculator).
